title: One Source, Every Format
text:
Preface: How to Use This Book
This book teaches a way of publishing in which you write once, in plain text, and every output rebuilds itself from that one source: a web page, a Word document, a PDF, slides, an e-book, a website, a blog and a dashboard. A coding assistant writes most of the code; you decide what to build, check what it wrote, and remain responsible for the result. The tool that turns the sources into outputs is Quarto, which is free and open source.
It grew out of a one-day workshop, and it keeps the workshop’s shape: two real projects, built step by step, with a way to catch up from any point. It also explains what the workshop only had time to show: why each step works, where it fails, and when not to take it.

title: One Source, Every Format
text:
Who this book is for
Researchers, analysts, students and anyone else who writes documents from data and is new to Quarto, to coding assistants or to both. Many readers will have little experience with a terminal, and Chapter 3 teaches the little you need. No programming is assumed: the book explains the Python the assistant writes, but you will not have to write it yourself.
You will need a computer on which you can install software (Windows, Mac or Linux), a free GitHub account, and access to one coding assistant, which requires a paid plan or an API key.

title: One Source, Every Format
text:
The two running examples
Every concept is tied to one of two projects, both built on real, cited data.
A London visitor guide (Part II). You work for the city’s tourism office and write one guide that becomes a web page, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, a dashboard for managers and a published website, with every visitor number computed from the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions’ published counts.
Drinking-water risk in Colombian municipalities (Part III). You group Colombia’s municipal zones into kinds by water safety, services and context, compare health and education outcomes between the kinds, and publish the analysis as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all from one analysis script. The data are Colombian open data, joined by official municipality codes.

How the book is organised
Part I covers what you need before the first project: what Quarto does (1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself), how to work with a coding assistant safely (2  Working With a Coding Assistant) and how to set up your computer (3  Setting Up Your Machine). Part II builds the London guide, from a first Markdown file to a published website, and ends by changing an input and explaining what the rebuild changed. Part III does the same for the water analysis, with the statistics explained on the way: exploring data, preparing features, clustering with k-means, interpreting the clusters and resisting a causal reading of them. The appendices hold the Windows setup, a cheatsheet, troubleshooting, every checkpoint, the data sources and an account of how this book itself is built.

When you fall behind
Every hands-on block ends at a checkpoint: a folder in the workshop repository (checkpoints/) holding the project as it should be at that point, with a README listing the steps to catch up. The workshop’s rule is simple: stuck for two minutes, catch up, and rejoin everyone at the next block. The same rule works alone. Each exercise ends with its catch-up line, which you paste into your assistant (Figure 1).






Figure 1: Catching up from a checkpoint. Your work is backed up first, so nothing is lost.



A checkpoint holds the end of its block, so it can be ahead of the step you were on: after catching up, skip the block’s remaining prompts and read on to the next exercise. The exercises at the end of each part, and Appendix E — Checkpoints at a Glance, and Answers, list every checkpoint.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.1 Why reports drift
Most reports are built by hand. An analyst runs a script, copies a number into a Word document, pastes a chart into a slide, retypes the same number in an email, and exports a PDF for the website. Every copy is a small act of faith that the number was right and is still right. When the data change, someone has to find every copy, and nobody can say for sure where each one came from.
This chapter is about the alternative this book teaches: one source that rebuilds every output. It explains what Quarto is and what happens when it renders a document, why it is deliberately not an AI tool even though this book uses one alongside it, and what “reproducible” does and does not promise. It ends with the cases where Quarto is the wrong choice, because a tool you cannot argue against is a tool you do not understand yet.
The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem. The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, and later a white paper. In the finished project, 5 pages read the same table of attraction visits, and between them they write 10 files: the guide alone becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a set of slides.
Suppose the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions (ALVA), the source of those counts, corrects one figure. In a copy-and-paste workflow, that correction has to reach 10 files by hand. Three things tend to go wrong:
None of these is a failure of care. They are what happens when the output is treated as the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source, and let a program rebuild the outputs.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.2 What Quarto is
Quarto is an open-source publishing system: a command-line program that turns plain-text source files into finished documents. It is free for anyone to use; the Quarto command-line tool has been under the MIT License since version 1.4 (GNU GPL v2 before that), and the tools it bundles have their own open-source licences (Quarto licence page, checked 2026-11-06).
The input is either a plain Markdown file (.md) or a Quarto document (.qmd). A .qmd file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at the top, written in YAML, and code cells, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built. Here is a complete one, the file the test run in Chapter 3 asks your assistant to write:
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{python}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{python} answer`.
The sentence at the bottom contains inline code: when the document is built, Quarto runs answer and writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same calculation gave 42, and that number was computed, not typed.

1.2.1 Three steps: execute, convert, typeset
quarto render does three things in order (Figure 1.1).






Figure 1.1: What quarto render does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.




Execute. A computation engine runs the code cells. For Python, that engine is Jupyter; for R, it is knitr. Quarto’s other principal languages are Julia and Observable JavaScript, which runs in the reader’s browser, and Jupyter kernels add many more. The results (numbers, tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file. This book uses Python only.
Convert. Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that Markdown once and writes each requested format: HTML, Word (docx), EPUB, PowerPoint (pptx) or a Reveal.js slide deck.
Typeset. For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF. No LaTeX installation is needed. (Quarto can also make PDFs through LaTeX, format: pdf, if you install a TeX distribution.)

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of your code: a missing package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a failure of the document: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.






NoteWhy this works



Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other. Both come from the same structured intermediate, so a heading is a heading everywhere.

The official list of formats is long and grouped by kind (Quarto, All Formats, checked 2026-10-30):

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.3 Quarto is not AI
This book pairs Quarto with a coding assistant, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding: that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software. Given the same source files and the same data, it writes the same outputs every time. It does not generate text, code or figures of its own, and it sends nothing to an AI service.
The assistant is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:



Table 1.2: Two tools with different failure modes.











Coding assistant
Quarto




Output for the same input
varies from run to run
identical


Typical mistake
plausible but wrong code or prose
a precise, reproducible error


How you check it
read its changes, run them, compare with the data
read the rendered output






Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the assistant makes lands in a file you can read before anything is published. And because the render is repeatable, anyone can rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the assistant at all.






WarningCommon pitfall



Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
1.4 Reproducible: same source, same result
Reproducible is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:
One source. Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important exists only inside an application.
Numbers are computed. Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code cell or inline code that reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.
One command. quarto render rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual export steps to remember.
Versioned. Git, the version-control tool installed in Chapter 3, records each saved state of the source, data and settings as a commit with a message saying why it changed. Any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be tied to the exact files that made it. The project’s Python packages are pinned too, in a lockfile (uv.lock, introduced in Chapter 4), so a colleague’s machine builds the same environment as yours.
Together these turn the drift problem around. Correct one value in the data, render, and the table, the chart and the sentence that quote it all update together, in every format.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?
Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.








WarningCommon pitfall



Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors findable, because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check results against their sources. Chapter 13 is an extended example of a result that reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.


There is one more subtlety, which matters once projects grow. Rendering every page from scratch can be slow, so Quarto can cache results with a setting called freeze. A cache is only as good as its rule for throwing results away, and Quarto re-executes a frozen page when that page’s source changes, not when a data file it reads changes. Chapter 14 shows how to use the cache safely. This book itself uses one, with a documented way to clear it (Appendix H).

section: 1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
text:
1.5 When Quarto is the wrong tool
Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

Collaborators who edit in Word. If the people who revise the document work in a word processor with tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have to be carried back into the source by hand. For documents whose main work is multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may simply fit better.
Designed layouts. Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs, figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
Format fidelity at the edges. Each format can only carry what it supports. Pandoc writes good Word and PowerPoint files, but a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, for example, so the London guide’s photo table shows each photo’s alt text in its pptx version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
One-off documents. A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains little from a build system.







TipIn practice



A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask “where did this number come from?”, the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is likely, use whatever is fastest.

title: 1  Publishing That Rebuilds Itself
text:
Summary
Reports drift because their outputs are edited by hand. Quarto removes the copies: a .qmd source holds text, settings and code; quarto render executes the code, converts the result with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets it with Typst. Quarto is deterministic software, separate from the coding assistant that writes its sources, and that separation is what makes an assistant’s mistakes inspectable. Reproducibility rests on one source, computed numbers, one command and version control; it makes results checkable, not automatically right. Use Quarto when a document will be rebuilt, and something simpler when it will not.

title: 2  Working With a Coding Assistant
text:
2.1 Model plus harness
Quarto turns sources into outputs, but someone still has to write the sources: the Markdown, the settings, and above all the code that reads data and draws charts. In this book that someone is usually a coding assistant, a program that writes and edits files and runs commands at your request. You describe the work, it does the typing, and you decide whether the result is right.
That division of labour is powerful, and it has sharp edges. An assistant can produce in a minute what would take an hour by hand, and it can produce plausible, confident, wrong work just as quickly. This chapter explains how assistants work, how to choose one and what it costs, where its reach begins and ends, how to give it rules that last, how to ask for work, and how to account for its use when the work is research. The rest of the book assumes all of it.
A coding assistant is two programs working together (Figure 2.1).
The model is a large language model, such as Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT or Google’s Gemini. It runs on the vendor’s servers. It reads text and writes text, and it can reply with a structured request to use a tool: “read this file”, “run this command”.
The harness is the program on your computer that surrounds the model. Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity are harnesses. The harness gives the model its tools (reading and writing files, running commands, searching), carries out the model’s tool requests, asks you before it does anything consequential, and sends the results back to the model. That loop repeats until the model replies with an answer instead of another request.
A short way to remember the split: the model decides, the harness does, you direct and check. It has a practical consequence. Many harnesses can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently inside a different harness. When an assistant disappoints you, the cause can be either half, and the fix is different: a stronger model for reasoning that falls short, better rules or permissions for a harness that does the wrong thing.

Other assistants exist; this book does not test them, so it does not list them. Every prompt in the book is written to work in any of the three. A vendor’s own pairing of harness and model is the easiest to set up, but it is not automatically the best fit for a task: the assistant and the model are separate choices.

2.2.1 Pick a model by task, not by rank
Each vendor offers a family of models, from small and cheap to large and capable. They are not simply better and worse versions of one thing. Larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from their own errors better. Small models are faster and cheaper, and often good enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Joining two datasets or debugging a failed render rewards the stronger model.
The prompts in this book are short and specific, so a mid-sized model at a moderate effort setting (how long the model reasons before answering) is enough: Claude’s Haiku or Sonnet on medium effort, or OpenAI’s Sol on low. For unfamiliar, hard work, the vendors’ own advice starts higher: Anthropic suggests starting with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. Start small, and move up only when a task keeps failing.

The cost of a fixed level of capability has been falling fast. Both warn that the pace may slow, and neither measures the frontier, where the price of the most capable work may fall more slowly. The practical lesson is the same either way: choose by what the task needs, not by today’s price.

Read the grid in two directions. Down the rows, the model grows and the price per token rises, so costs climb from fractions of a cent to more than ten cents. text:
2.3 What a conversation costs
Models are paid for by the token, a fragment of text of a few characters. Three things raise the cost of a session:

A bigger model costs more per token.
A higher effort setting makes the model write more reasoning tokens per reply.
A longer conversation costs more with every turn, because the model keeps no memory between requests: the harness sends the whole conversation again each time. Prompt caching makes the repeated part cheaper, not free, and caches expire.

The habits that follow are simple: a mid-sized model at moderate effort, one task per conversation, and a fresh conversation as soon as a task is done. Three commands, typed at the assistant’s prompt rather than in the shell, cover them:



Table 2.2: Three commands that control cost and context (Claude Code commands reference and Codex CLI reference, checked 2026-11-12). Type / alone to list your assistant’s commands.











Command
Claude Code
Codex
Use it when




/model
switches the model; arrows adjust the effort level where the model supports it
chooses the model and reasoning effort
a prompt keeps failing (go up) or the work is routine (go down)


/clear
starts a new conversation with empty context; the old one can be resumed
clears the terminal and starts a fresh chat
a task is finished and an unrelated one starts


/exit
exits; /quit is the same
exits; /quit is the same
you are done, or need to move to another folder






/clear matters for quality as well as cost. Old instructions and files read earlier keep steering the model while they remain in the conversation; a fresh conversation drops them. Nothing on disk changes, and the project’s rules file is read again.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. One task is finished and an unrelated one starts. Which command first?
/clear. The new task needs none of the old conversation, and carrying it along costs tokens on every turn and can mislead the model.

section: 2.4 The root folder is the assistant’s world
text:
2.4 The root folder is the assistant’s world
An assistant treats the folder you start it in as its root: it reads and edits files there and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a new folder, it asks whether you trust it. Claude Code’s prompt, captured on 2026-11-07, warns that “Claude Code’ll be able to read, edit, and execute files here”; Codex asks the same question in a folder that is a Git repository, and says it can read, edit and run files “subject to your permission settings”.
That question deserves a real answer. Trust only a folder you created for the work. Never start an assistant in your home folder, in Documents, or anywhere that holds other people’s projects, private documents or keys (such as ~/.ssh). Project instructions in a trusted folder are read and followed too, which is another reason to trust only your own folders.
Starting in a small project folder has three practical benefits. Paths in prompts stay short (data/attractions.csv), the project’s rules file is found, and a mistake stays inside one folder that you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary, though: a command can still name a path outside the folder, so read each command before you approve it.






WarningCommon pitfall



Two assistants writing to the same folder at once will overwrite each other’s work and collide when both render. To work on another project, leave with /exit, change folder, and start the assistant again there.

text:
2.5 Rules that persist: AGENTS.md
Everything you tell an assistant in conversation is forgotten when the conversation ends. Rules that must hold in every session go in a file: AGENTS.md, a plain Markdown file at the top of the project folder that the assistant reads at the start of each session. A good one has three parts:

Scope: what the project is, and what it is not.
Rules: what must always hold (“every number comes from a cited file in data/”).
Commands: how to build and check the project.

All three assistants in this book read it (checked 2026-10-30). Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work. Antigravity reads AGENTS.md or GEMINI.md in the project’s folders. Claude Code reads AGENTS.md when there is no CLAUDE.md in the working folder or above it, from version 2.1.277; a CLAUDE.md whose first line is @AGENTS.md imports it, so one file can serve all three (Claude Code memory documentation, checked 2026-11-12). The repository behind this book works exactly that way: its CLAUDE.md imports its AGENTS.md.






WarningCommon pitfall



AGENTS.md is context, not enforcement. The assistant reads the rules and usually follows them, but it can still slip. Write rules that are concrete enough to check (“call ALVA counts ‘ALVA member attractions’”), and check them.


Part II writes the London guide’s rules in Chapter 4, and Part III writes the water analysis’s in Chapter 8.

text:
2.6 How to ask for work
A prompt is the request you type into the assistant. Four habits make prompts reliable:
Be specific. Name the files, the columns, the chart type and the output. “Make a chart” invites guessing; “add a horizontal bar chart of visits_2025 by attraction from data/attractions.csv” does not.
One step at a time. One task per prompt keeps each change small enough to review, and tells you which step broke when one does.
Ask it to run and check. End with a check the assistant can perform: “render it and tell me which file it wrote”, “check that the PDF is one page”. An assistant that verifies its own work catches many of its own mistakes.
Check what changed. You are responsible for the result. Read the changed files (most assistants can show you a diff, the lines added and removed) before moving on.
The prompts in this book were designed with AI assistance and refined to reduce errors, but they are not magic, and assistants vary. When a prompt mentions something you do not understand, a YAML key, a Markdown construct, a Python call, ask before you paste:



Ask your coding assistant

Explain what a Markdown table is and when to use it. Then name the official docs page where I can verify your answer.


Asking for the documentation page matters: it turns the answer into something you can check.

2.6.1 A web chat can draft your prompt
If you know what you want but not how to ask for it, a free web chat (Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude in the browser) can turn a rough idea into a prompt. Describe the goal in plain words, name your tools, and ask for a prompt of one to four lines, with one task, concrete file names and a check (Figure 2.3). The chat cannot see your files, so it guesses; the assistant can see them, so it checks. Read the drafted prompt before you paste it, and fix any file name that does not match your folder.






Figure 2.3: A web chat drafts a prompt, you read it, and the coding assistant runs it. An illustration drawn for the workshop, not a recording: real replies vary.









WarningCommon pitfall



Paste only what you would be happy to publish. Web chats and assistants send your text to the vendor: no passwords, keys, unpublished data or personal information.

section: 2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
text:
2.8 Using AI in research: say it, own it
If your work is research, using an assistant raises obligations beyond getting the code right. Journals and funders differ in detail, so read your venue’s own policy, but the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE), whose recommendations many journals follow, states a common core (checked 2026-11-12):

An AI tool is never an author. Chatbots and other AI-assisted tools “should not be listed as authors because they cannot be responsible for the accuracy, integrity, and originality of the work”.
You are responsible for what it produced. Humans are responsible for any submitted material that used AI-assisted technologies, and should review and edit AI output, which “can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased”. That includes references: AI-generated material is not an acceptable primary source.
Disclose the use. Authors describe their use of AI-assisted technologies at submission, in the cover letter and in the appropriate section of the work.

Two further rules follow from ordinary research ethics rather than from any one policy. Keep unpublished manuscripts, participant data and other confidential material out of public AI tools. And never let a tool generate or alter primary data or images: presenting generated data as observed is fabrication.
A useful disclosure names the tool and version, the tasks it performed and the checks you made. The statement for this book, on its copyright page, is written that way. Where it goes depends on the use: code and analysis belong in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them, which in a Quarto project means the code itself and the project’s AGENTS.md.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table?
Computing a table is analysis: describe it in the Methods, in enough detail to reproduce. Venues differ on whether language editing needs a statement; ICMJE’s recommendations make no exception for it, so when in doubt, disclose.

Summary
A coding assistant is a model that decides and a harness that acts, with you directing and checking in between. Choose the model by the task: mid-sized models at moderate effort are enough for well-specified steps, and the price of a given capability is falling fast. Cost grows with model size, effort and conversation length, so keep one task per conversation and start fresh between tasks. Start the assistant only in a folder you created for the work, and put durable rules in AGENTS.md, remembering that rules are context, not enforcement. Good prompts are specific, single-step and end in a check, and every change they cause is yours to review. In research, the assistant is never an author, and its use is disclosed.

text:
3.1 Before you start
Everything in Parts II and III happens on your own computer: the assistant writes files in your folders, Quarto renders them there, and you open the results in your own browser and word processor. This chapter gets that computer ready in six steps. Each step ends with a check you can see, so you always know whether it worked before you move on, and the last one, a test run, proves that the tools work together by printing the number 42 in a web page and a PDF.
Do the setup somewhere calm, with a good connection and an hour to spare: the six steps are timed at 48 minutes in the workshop, done at home. Mac and Linux readers can follow this chapter straight through. Windows readers first install Ubuntu, a version of Linux, inside Windows with WSL; Appendix A walks through that one step at a time, and from then on they follow this chapter inside Ubuntu.
A stable, fast connection. Almost every step downloads something: on Windows the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes), then Quarto, uv and Python packages, the assistant itself and the workshop’s data. The assistant also sends every request to its model over the internet, so a weak connection shows up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which are easy to mistake for your own errors. Use a wired connection or strong Wi-Fi, avoid VPNs where you can, and expect company networks with a proxy to block some downloads.
Two accounts. A free GitHub account, used to publish in Parts II and III, and an account with access to one coding assistant. Claude Code needs a Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account; Codex a ChatGPT sign-in or an API key; Antigravity a Google account (checked 2026-11-03). Sign-up and email verification can take hours, so do them first.
A way to get unstuck. Installs fail before the assistant is working, and sometimes the assistant is what fails, so you need a route that does not depend on it: a free web chat in your browser. Copy the command you ran and the whole error message, paste both with a sentence saying your system (“Mac”, or “Windows with Ubuntu on WSL”) and which step you are on, and try one suggested fix at a time. Read each suggested command before you run it, and never paste passwords, keys or private data. If two suggestions fail, ask a person: your group’s help channel, or a colleague.

3.2 Step 1: Get the computer ready
The later steps assume two small programs: git, for version control, and curl, for downloading. Open a terminal (on a Mac: Command-Space, type Terminal, Enter; on Ubuntu: Ctrl+Alt+T) and run the line for your system.
On a Mac, install Apple’s Command Line Tools, which include git:
xcode-select --install
A dialog asks to install them: click Install and wait. Doing this deliberately now matters, because otherwise the dialog appears the first time anything uses git, which would be in the middle of Step 4 while the assistant is waiting. “Already installed” is fine.
On Ubuntu or Debian (including Ubuntu on Windows):
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git
sudo runs a command as the administrator and asks for your Linux password, which stays invisible as you type. On other Linux distributions, install curl and git with your usual package manager. On Windows, follow Appendix A first: it ends with this same command, run inside Ubuntu.

Run git --version in the terminal.

3.3 Step 2: Move around the terminal
The rest of the book happens in a terminal, a window where you type commands instead of clicking. When it is ready for a command it shows a prompt, a line ending in $ (or % on a Mac), which tells you who and where you are:
ana@laptop:~/demo$
ana is the user, laptop the computer, and ~/demo the current folder: ~ is your home folder, so this is a folder called demo inside it. Eight commands are enough to move around:



Table 3.2: Moving around the terminal.









Command
Does




pwd
prints the folder you are in (print working directory)


date
prints the date and time


ls
lists what is in this folder


mkdir name
makes a folder


cd name
goes into a folder


cd ..
goes up one folder


cd ~
goes straight home, from anywhere


rmdir name
removes an empty folder (it refuses if anything is inside)






Figure 3.1 runs them in order. Type them yourself rather than pasting: the hands remember.






Figure 3.1: Moving around the terminal: each command, and what the terminal answers. A real recording, made with a demo account whose home folder is /tmp/home/ana; yours is /home/<you> on Linux and Windows, or /Users/<you> on a Mac.



Two keys save most typing mistakes: Tab completes a file or folder name, and the up arrow brings back the previous command. Later chapters use one compound command often:
mkdir -p london-guide && cd london-guide
-p makes mkdir quietly accept a folder that already exists, and && means “and then, if that worked”. Appendix B (Appendix B) has more keys and habits.






ImportantTry it



From your home folder, type the commands in Table 3.2 in the order shown in Figure 3.1.

You're done when rmdir raised no error, and the prompt shows ~.




3.3.1 Two places to type
Once an assistant is running, there are two places to type, and mixing them up costs beginners more time than anything else.
ana@laptop:~/setup$ pwd                  <- the terminal: commands
❯ Which tools are missing?                <- the assistant: requests in plain language
The assistant takes over the terminal tab it runs in: what you type there goes to the assistant, not to the shell, until you leave with /exit. Commands in this book’s You do boxes, such as quarto preview, go in the terminal; prompts in Ask your coding assistant boxes go to the assistant. When the assistant is busy and you need the terminal, open a second tab (Ctrl+Shift+T on Ubuntu, Command-T on a Mac, Ctrl+Shift+D in Windows Terminal).
Typing in the wrong place is usually harmless: a prompt typed at $ gives command not found, and a command typed into the assistant is read as a request. Look at the line you are on and try again.






TipIn practice



Pause and think. The assistant is running and the book says to type gh auth login. Where do you type it?
In a second terminal tab: gh auth login is an interactive sign-in that needs you, and the assistant is using the first tab. Leaving the assistant with /exit also works, but ends the conversation.

Pick one assistant and run its installer, the vendor’s own documented command (checked 2026-10-30):

# Codex

# Antigravity
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash

Then open a new terminal tab. A terminal learns where programs are when it starts, so it cannot find one installed a moment ago, which is the usual cause of command not found straight after an install. On a Mac, Claude Code’s installer prints a line to add to your settings under “Setup notes”: paste it, then open the new tab.

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup
claude          # or: codex, or: agy

Sign in. Choose the first option, a subscription account. The assistant opens your browser; where there is none, as in WSL, it prints a link to copy into your browser, and then a code to paste back into the terminal.

3.5 Step 4: Let the assistant install the tools
The remaining tools are Quarto itself, uv (which manages Python for each project), Git and the GitHub command-line tool gh. Each has its own official install method for each system, which is exactly the kind of detail an assistant handles well. Start it again in the setup folder:

mkdir -p ~/setup && cd ~/setup && claude

Check which of `git`, `curl`, `uv`, `quarto` (1.10 or newer) and the GitHub CLI `gh` are missing on this computer. Install only those, using each tool's official method for my system. installs uv with its official installer · Quarto from its release page (or Homebrew on a Mac) · gh from GitHub’s own package source · prints versions


The prompt is written around one limitation: an assistant cannot type your password. So it asks the assistant to hand back any command that needs one, with full paths, because the second tab you paste it into starts in your home folder. Paste the command there, type your password when sudo asks (it stays invisible), and then type done in the assistant’s tab. On a Mac, the password is your login password.






NoteWhy this works



Quarto has no Ubuntu package in the standard repositories, and Ubuntu’s own gh package is discouraged by GitHub, so a generic apt install would get one tool wrong and the other missing. The prompt’s “each tool’s official method” sends the assistant to the right source for each (Quarto’s download page and GitHub’s install instructions for Linux, checked 2026-10-30).

Paste the prompt, approve the commands you have read, and run any sudo command it hands you in a second tab.

Open a new tab and start the assistant again, so that it sees the newly installed tools:

Print the versions of `quarto` (1.10 or newer), `uv`, `gh` and this assistant, and run `quarto check` (no Jupyter or LaTeX yet is fine: count it as OK). Its Python and Jupyter lines may say they are missing, and that is fine: each project in this book gets its own Python environment from uv, so there is nothing to install for Python now. No LaTeX is needed either, because PDFs are made with the Typst engine bundled in Quarto.
A fresh Git has no identity, and git commit refuses to run without one. The prompt makes the assistant ask you for your name and email, so you type your own; check that what it set is yours, not a placeholder.
The clone brings the workshop repository to ~/quarto-workshop. It holds the finished examples, the water dataset and the checkpoints: snapshots of each project at the end of each hands-on block, which you will use to catch up if you fall behind.

if gh is not “Logged in”: in a second tab, gh auth login → GitHub.com → HTTPS → Yes → log in with a web browser; copy the one-time code to github.com/login/device; then ask the assistant to check gh again

The setup check proves the tools are installed. The test run proves they work together: the assistant can write a file and run commands you approve, uv can build a project environment, Quarto can run Python through it, and Typst can write a PDF.



You do

mkdir -p ~/quarto-test && cd ~/quarto-test
claude

Run `uv init --bare` and `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml`. Create hello.qmd (html and typst formats): a Python cell computing `6 * 7` and an inline-code sentence showing it. Render it with `uv run quarto render hello.qmd`; check hello.html and hello.pdf both say 42.

uv init --bare · uv add … · writes hello.qmd · uv run quarto render hello.qmd → hello.html, hello.pdf



You do

/exit, then open the folder: open . (Mac), xdg-open . (Linux) or explorer.exe . (WSL), and open both files

It is harmless: Quarto talks to the Python kernel over a local connection on your own computer, and in every dry run the warning came with a successful render and changed nothing in the output.

Run the test run and open both outputs.

title: 4  Markdown, Rendering and Project Rules
text:
4.1 The brief and the folder
The London guide starts as an empty folder and, by the end of this chapter, is a web page built from a plain-text file, with a written contract for the assistant and a Python environment ready for the code that follows. That is the first workshop block, and it is the one where most recovery happens, because everything is new at once: the assistant, the rules, the preview and the environment.
The source format throughout is Markdown, a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks. It matters that you can read it, even though the assistant writes most of it: Markdown is the layer you review, compare between versions and fix by hand when a sentence is wrong. This chapter introduces it one construct at a time, each with the prompt that adds it to the guide.

4.4 Rules for the guide
Section 2.5 introduced AGENTS.md, the file of rules an assistant reads at the start of every session. The guide needs one now, before any data or photos arrive, because every later prompt relies on it:



Ask your coding assistant

Create AGENTS.md for this project. Scope: a London visitor guide for the tourism office, written once and reused for every audience. Rules: every number comes from a cited file in data/, photos are openly licensed, credited and show no people, never invent facts, keep data/ and images/ unchanged, and call ALVA counts "ALVA member attractions". Show me the file.



Expect it to run

writes AGENTS.md: a scope and a list of rules



You do

approve · read it: does it say what you meant?


Each rule is there for a reason the project will meet. Every number comes from a cited file: the guide quotes visitor counts, and an assistant asked for a number it does not have may produce a plausible one; a rule that every figure is computed from a file with a source removes that temptation, and gives you something to check. Openly licensed photos with no people: a published guide needs images it may reuse, and pictures of identifiable people raise consent questions it does not need. Keep data/ and images/ unchanged: the inputs are evidence, and edits belong in the analysis, not in the evidence. “ALVA member attractions”: the counts come from the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions, which lists only its members, so “London’s most visited attractions” would overclaim.
The finished project’s version reads, in part:
## Rules

- Every number comes from a cited file in `data/`: each row carries `source`, `url` and
  `retrieved`. Never estimate or invent a figure or a fact.
- ALVA counts only its member sites: write "ALVA member attractions".
- Photos are openly licensed, credited from `images/ATTRIBUTION.md`, and show no people.
- Keep `data/` and `images/` unchanged.
Read what the assistant wrote and edit it yourself if the wording is off. It is your project’s contract with the assistant, and the rules work best when they are concrete enough to check.

text:
4.9 Environments, then and now
The next chapter runs Python, and code never runs in a vacuum. It runs on an operating system (macOS, Windows, Linux) and a processor (Intel and AMD x86_64, or Apple and other ARM arm64), in some version of its language, with packages at particular versions. Many scientific Python packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each system and processor, and Python’s packaging encodes both in each package file’s platform tag, such as macosx_11_0_arm64 (Python Packaging Authority, checked 2026-10-31).
Getting all of that to agree used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix the PATH, register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on every laptop. uv now does it in one step, for one project at a time. It fetches the Python version a project needs, and its lockfile, uv.lock, “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (uv documentation, checked 2026-10-31), so one file reproduces the same environment on every Mac, Windows and Linux machine. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile in the same way: R’s renv.lock, JavaScript’s package-lock.json, Rust’s Cargo.lock.



Ask your coding assistant

Give this folder its own Python environment with `uv`: run `uv init --bare`, then `uv add ipykernel nbclient nbformat pyyaml pandas matplotlib plotly`. From now on run `quarto` and `python` through `uv run`, and add that rule to AGENTS.md. Show me the Python line of `uv run quarto check jupyter`.



Expect it to run

writes pyproject.toml (the packages), uv.lock (their exact versions) and .venv/ (the installed environment) · adds a rule to AGENTS.md








Figure 4.3: Giving the guide its own environment: uv init --bare, uv add with the guide’s packages, and Quarto finding the project’s own Python. A real recording with a demo account; the 40-second first render of the engine check is cut.



The four packages ipykernel, nbclient, nbformat and pyyaml are what Quarto needs to run Python cells; pandas, matplotlib and plotly are what the guide’s code will use. The larger jupyter package, with its notebook applications, is not needed. On the workshop’s dry run (2026-10-30), a cold install of Part III’s larger package set took 8 seconds with uv and 31 seconds with pip and jupyter, on one fast connection.






NoteWhy this works



Why uv run in front of every command? Quarto refuses to run Python next to a .venv folder that is not activated (“There is an unactivated Python environment in .venv”). uv run activates the project’s environment for that one command, and first brings .venv up to date with uv.lock. So a copied project, or a checkpoint, rebuilds its own environment on its first uv run, and the rule in AGENTS.md keeps the assistant using it after a restart.

Run the environment prompt. Keep the preview running: london.md needs no Python yet.

4.10 When you fall behind
You will get stuck at some point: a prompt that goes wrong, a file you cannot repair, an environment that will not build. The book’s routine, from the workshop, is to spend two minutes on it and then catch up, rather than debugging while the material moves on.



Ask your coding assistant

Catch me up: follow ../quarto-workshop/checkpoints/01-london-markdown/README.md

The checkpoint’s README lists the steps, which you can also run by hand (Figure 4.4): back up the folder, copy the checkpoint into it, render, check a named output, and rejoin. Nothing is lost: each backup is a new folder named with the date and time, so earlier backups are kept.






Figure 4.4: Catching up by hand, as the checkpoint’s README lists it: a time-stamped backup of the folder (all but .venv/), the checkpoint copied in, and a render that rebuilds the environment from uv.lock first. A real recording with a demo account.









NoteWhy this works



The backup leaves out .venv/ because it can hold hundreds of megabytes and is rebuilt from uv.lock on the next uv run. Copying it would be slow and pointless. A checkpoint is the state at the end of its block, so it can include steps you have not reached: after catching up, skip the block’s remaining prompts and read on to the next exercise.

text:
5.1 From .md to .qmd: YAML front matter
So far the guide is text someone typed. This chapter turns it into a document that computes: settings at the top, code that reads the data, numbers in sentences that come from that code, and a chart that is drawn from the same table. Then one source becomes three formats, and optionally six, without a single number copied by hand.
This is the chapter where the workflow’s central promise becomes concrete. Once a number is computed rather than typed, correcting the data corrects every place the number appears, in every format, at the next render. The rest of the book builds on that.
Front matter is a block of settings between two lines of three dashes at the very top of a file. It is written in YAML, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning: nested settings are indented by two spaces, and a wrong indent changes what a setting belongs to. A .qmd file is Markdown plus front matter plus code; the extension tells Quarto to look for both.

text:
5.6 What a render does, and why two renders collide
Figure 1.1 in Section 1.2 showed the three steps of a render. With code in the document, the first step is worth looking at more closely, because it explains the commonest failure of this chapter.
To run the cells, Quarto writes the document out as a temporary Jupyter notebook, named after the file (london.quarto_ipynb), starts a Python kernel (a running Python process) from the project’s environment, sends it each cell in order, and collects the results. Two consequences follow. The cells share one Python session, top to bottom, so a later cell can use a variable from an earlier one, and the order of cells matters. And two renders of the same file at the same moment write the same temporary files, which is why a render started while a preview is re-rendering fails with readfile 'london.quarto_ipynb'.
Every render runs every cell again. That is deliberate in this book’s projects: they set freeze: false, so outputs always match the data. It also means a slow cell slows every render; Chapter 14 returns to the trade-off and to freeze: auto, which caches results and needs a rule for when to throw them away.






WarningCommon pitfall



Every render prints [IPKernelApp] WARNING | Kernel is running over TCP without encryption. It is harmless: the “TCP” connection is between Quarto and a Python process on your own computer.








ImportantTry it



Stop the preview, then add the formats with the prompt in Section 5.4 (and, if you like, the optional three).

text:
6.1 Content once, format per audience
A tourism office does not have one reader. Managers want to see the numbers at a glance, partners want a document they can forward, people walking past the office want something to take away, and visitors want a website. Writing each of those by hand is how the same fact ends up four ways in four places.
This chapter writes the guide once more, in three new forms at the same time: a dashboard, a Word brief with its covering email, and a printed flyer. All three read the same data, so one correction reaches all of them. Because the three are independent, they are also the first task in this book worth splitting across several assistants working in parallel, and the chapter explains when that is a good idea and when it is not. It ends with an optional look at the same data in three dimensions.
Each audience gets the format that suits it, and each format is a setting:
A dashboard is a page of charts and key numbers arranged in a grid. In a .qmd file with format: dashboard, a level-1 heading starts a page, a level-2 heading starts a row, and each cell’s output becomes a card in that row (Quarto dashboards documentation, checked 2026-10-31). The guide’s dashboard has two pages:
It also needs a second data file. data/visits.csv holds the yearly visits to the five sights from 2015 to 2025, from ALVA’s annual tables. Two notes travel with it, from the data’s README: 2020 and 2021 are pandemic years and not comparable with the others, and from 2024 the Natural History Museum’s count includes its reopened gardens, so 2024 and 2025 are not like-for-like with earlier years for that museum. data/churches.csv lists the 10 cathedrals and churches on Visit London’s own list, an editorial choice with no visitor numbers.
A Word brief turns Markdown headings into Word’s heading styles, so the partner’s copy has a navigable outline and working links. Its covering email is not rendered at all: it is a plain Markdown file whose message sits in a text block, to be copied into an email client, with the brief attached. The email deliberately quotes no visitor numbers. The numbers stay in the brief, where they are computed and cited, as the project’s rules require.
A flyer is a one-page Typst PDF on A5 paper. papersize accepts any of Typst’s paper names (a5, a4, us-letter and so on), and margin sets the margins (Quarto’s Typst documentation, checked 2026-10-30).

text:
6.2 Sub-agents: one lead, many hands
The three outputs are independent: none needs another to exist. That makes them a candidate for sub-agents, separate assistant sessions that your assistant starts for one task each (Figure 6.3). Each sub-agent has its own context, does its task and reports back; your assistant, the lead, waits for all of them and then checks the results.






Figure 6.3: One lead, three sub-agents. Each writes only its own files and renders nothing; the lead renders the files one at a time.



The gain is time: three independent tasks take about as long as the slowest of them. The cost is tokens, because each sub-agent does its own reading, reasoning and tool calls. The three assistants differ in how they offer it (all checked 2026-10-31). Claude Code starts sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them; its own documentation’s example is “Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents”. Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked, and its documentation warns both that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens. Antigravity’s command-line agent can delegate to parallel sub-agents, but its documentation does not say a prompt can require it, so it may do the tasks itself.
Two rules make parallel work safe, and the prompt below states both. Each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, so no two of them touch the same file. The lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two environment updates by uv run, in the same folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules still apply to their work.






TipIn practice



Use sub-agents when tasks are independent, substantial and write different files. Do not use them for tasks where one needs another’s result, for several edits to the same file, or for small tasks where the overhead of starting and briefing a sub-agent outweighs the work. A prompt that might run without sub-agents should say what to do then: the prompt below ends its first line with “none? do the items in turn”.

“End each chart cell with fig” is there because of a failure seen in practice: a Plotly chart appears twice in a dashboard card when the cell both calls fig.show() and returns the figure. Assign the figure, end the cell with its name, and nothing else. If a chart’s legend looks clipped, ask for a horizontal legend with a fixed entrywidth; if the flyer spills onto a second page, ask for a smaller photo.

6.5.1 Asking for three.js
You do not need to know three.js to ask for it. Name the library, the data and what you want to do with the result, and check the numbers:



Ask your coding assistant

Create visits-3d.html with `three.js` from a CDN: a labelled 3-D bar per `attraction` in data/visits.csv, as tall as its `visits` in the latest `year`, that I can drag to turn. Put the numbers in the page so it opens by double-click, then check them against the CSV.

three.js is a free JavaScript library (MIT License) that draws 3-D scenes with the browser’s WebGL, so the reader installs nothing. Two details of the prompt matter. It asks for the numbers to be written into the page, because a page opened by double-click cannot read local files. And the page loads three.js from a content delivery network (CDN), so it needs the internet to work; a published page keeps that dependency, which is why this book, like the workshop’s slides, ships its own copy of the library.






WarningCommon pitfall



Be honest about 3-D charts. Perspective makes bars harder to compare than a plain bar chart: the near bar looks taller than an equal bar behind it. Figure 5.1 is the better chart for comparing visits. Use 3-D when the third dimension means something, as height does on a map, or for delight, and say which.

title: 7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
7.1 Git: every change, safely
The guide exists on your computer. This chapter puts it on the web, as a website anyone can open on a phone, and then asks the question the whole workflow is built to answer: if one input changes, which outputs change with it, and how do you know?
Publishing involves two new tools, Git for keeping every version of the source and GitHub Pages for serving the result, plus one decision about where the rendered site is built. The rebuild question has no prompt in this chapter. It is a test of whether you can predict what a rebuild will do, and then check.
A repository is a project folder together with its full history. Git records that history as commits: snapshots of every tracked file, each with a message saying why it changed, so any earlier version can be restored or compared with another. Six ideas cover how teams use it (Figure 7.1; Pro Git and GitHub’s documentation, checked 2026-10-31):
A branch is a movable label on a line of commits, so work can happen on a branch while the main line, called main, keeps working. Push copies commits to the shared repository on GitHub. A pull request proposes merging a branch and shows the difference, or diff, line by line; a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes; merging adds its commits to main.
Working alone, as in this book, you commit straight to main and push. In a team, every change goes round the loop; the repository behind this book is built that way. Either way, the assistant runs the Git commands and you approve them. Ask it to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diffs before you approve: the diff is the clearest view you will get of what the assistant actually did.

title: 7  Publishing and Proving the Rebuild
text:
7.2 Where a site lives
A rendered Quarto website is static: a folder of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images and documents, with no program running on a server. Any web server can serve it, so publishing means copying that folder to a host. GitHub Pages is the host this book uses, because the repository is already on GitHub and quarto publish gh-pages is built in (Figure 7.2).






Figure 7.2: Publishing to GitHub Pages. The source goes to the main branch with Git; quarto publish gh-pages renders the site on your computer and pushes only the rendered HTML to a separate branch, which GitHub serves.



There are two ways to get a site onto a host, and the difference matters. In the first, you render on your own computer and upload the result: quarto publish does this for GitHub Pages and Netlify. In the second, the host builds the site from your repository on every push. That only works if the build installs Quarto, Python and every package the project needs, or if the rendered output is committed. Since the London repository leaves its rendered _site/ folder out, connecting it to a host that builds would produce nothing until the build is set up.

7.4 Publish



Ask your coding assistant

Initialise a git repository here. Replace README.md in this folder with a short one linking to https://<your-github-username>.github.io/london-guide/ and listing the files in the site's Downloads menu. Commit everything except _site/, .quarto/, .venv/ and *_files/, then create a public GitHub repository named `london-guide` with gh and push to it. Expect it to run

git init · git add · git commit · gh repo create london-guide --public --source=. --push · gh repo edit --homepage …



You do

approve gh · in the second tab: uv run quarto publish gh-pages, then Enter at “Publish site … (Y/n)” · open the address on your phone · a 404? wait a minute and reload


The assistant creates the repository on GitHub from your folder and pushes the commits, using the sign-in from the setup check. The README it writes is what visitors to the repository see first, so its link takes them from the source to the live site.
The first publish is yours, typed in the terminal. It asks one question, then renders the site, creates the gh-pages branch, pushes the rendered site and opens it. Quarto’s GitHub Pages guide asks for one local, interactive publish before any automated one (checked 2026-11-01), and the workshop’s dry run on Quarto 1.6.40 showed why: with --no-prompt, the first publish stopped with “the remote origin does not have a branch named gh-pages”. Once the branch exists, the assistant can update the site with uv run quarto publish gh-pages --no-prompt.
In that dry run, the first publish of each site took about one and a half to two minutes from creating the branch to pushing the built site, and GitHub Pages then built it in 20 to 35 seconds. A 404 page in the first minute usually means the site is still being deployed.






WarningCommon pitfall



A push that fails with HTTP 400 (“RPC failed”, “the remote end hung up unexpectedly”) was seen with larger sites, such as dashboards with embedded maps. Raise Git’s buffer for this repository with git config http.postBuffer 524288000, and push again.








TipIn practice



Publishing from your own computer is simple and keeps the build where your environment is. The alternative is a GitHub Action that renders on every push, using Quarto’s quarto-dev/quarto-actions. It needs Python and the project’s packages installed in the job, or freeze set so that committed results are reused, and Quarto’s guide still asks for one local quarto publish gh-pages first.

Publish the guide.

Here is the test of everything so far, with no prompt supplied. Write your own, or do it by hand.

5 pages load attractions.csv, and between them they write 10 files, so the change reaches all of them at the next render. Every one of those pages finds the top attraction and the total with the same two calls, attractions["visits_2025"].idxmax() and .sum(), which is why the Tower of London becomes the top attraction everywhere at once.
Two rows deserve a second look. The flyer loads no data at all, and the guide’s table of sights loads sights.csv nowhere, although its credits name the file: both copy their facts (price bands, nearest stations) from the cited file into the Markdown. That was a reasonable choice, because those facts rarely change, but it means a correction to sights.csv updates neither of them. A cited copy is still a copy.






NoteWhy this works



Why does every page recompute, even ones whose sources did not change? Because the project renders with freeze: false: every render re-runs every page’s code. That is what makes the answer to this exercise simple. With caching turned on, a page whose own source did not change would keep its old numbers, and the answer would depend on the cache. Chapter 14 returns to that trade-off.

The same data can also become an academic paper: an abstract, numbered sections, computed results and a reference list, set in the typeface LaTeX documents use, without installing LaTeX.

1    mainfont: "New Computer Modern"
2    section-numbering: "1.1"

WarningCommon pitfall

An inline expression in a YAML abstract runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract in the body, in a raw Typst block. title: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications
text:
Which kinds of municipality exist in Colombia, judged by the safety of their drinking water, their services and their context? And how do infant mortality, exam scores and school dropout differ between those kinds? Part III answers both questions with real public data, then publishes the answer as a report, slides, a blog post and a website, all reading the results of one analysis script.
The unit of analysis is one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year, so a municipality’s two zones can belong to different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years. The project lives beside the London one:
~                      your home folder
├── quarto-workshop/   the clone from Chapter 3
├── london-guide/      Part II
└── water-quality/     this part's project



Where we are: Part III.
crumbs: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.1 Why drinking water
Part II’s numbers were simple counts; Part III’s are not. The question is about public health and education in Colombia, the data come from five government sources joined on official codes, and the analysis groups places by statistical similarity and then compares outcomes between the groups. Every step has a way to go wrong that a clean render will not reveal: a variable that means something narrower than its name, a gap that is not random, a comparison that looks causal and is not.
So this chapter does the work that comes before any code: what the question is and why it is worth asking, what the two key measures mean, where the data come from and what one row represents, which variables may define the groups and which may only describe them, and how the project is built so that one analysis feeds every publication. It ends, as Part II began, with the project’s rules and environment.
Colombia measures the safety of drinking water with the IRCA, the Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano (water-quality risk index for human consumption), defined in Resolución 2115 of 2007. Surveillance samples of tap water are tested against health limits. Each tested characteristic carries a risk score: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6 and pH 1.5, among others. A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit, as a percentage of the score of all those tested, and a month’s IRCA is the mean over its samples (articles 13 and 14). So 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed. Article 15 sorts the scale into five bands (Table 8.1).
The national average sits in the medium band, but averages hide where the risk is: urban water is low-risk on average and rural water high-risk. That gap is the reason to look at municipalities and their urban and rural zones separately, and the reason this part’s data are organised that way.

WarningCommon pitfall



The IRCA in this part’s data is not the national figure. The open table it comes from (INS, datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3) holds the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA: samples from systems run by a water utility. A check on 2026-10-30 found that its 2023 department totals match INCA’s utility column in 30 of 30 departments and the overall figure in only 5. title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.2 Two measures: IRCA and Saber 11
The outcomes the analysis compares include an education measure, Saber 11, the national exam taken by students finishing upper secondary school, set by ICFES. It has five tests: critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, and English. The global score is five times the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0 to 100; English counts once, the others three times), from 0 to 500, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting in 2014, so that years can be compared (ICFES, Guía de orientación Saber 11.° 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104, checked 2026-10-30).
Both measures are averages, and an average describes only what it averaged over. IRCA is an average over the water samples taken, so a system that is never sampled has no IRCA at all. The Saber 11 mean in the data is an average over the students who sat the exam in a municipality’s schools, so it says nothing about students who had left school. Keep both facts in mind in every comparison that follows.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.3 Where the data come from
All the data are Colombian open data, joined on DANE’s DIVIPOLA municipality codes:

INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud): the IRCA surveillance results.
DANE (the national statistics office): the list of municipalities and their codes, population projections and municipal boundaries.
ICFES and MEN (the Ministry of Education): Saber 11 results and school dropout rates.
DNP (the National Planning Department), through its TerriData portal: water and sewer coverage, multidimensional poverty, municipal performance, transfers for water and infant mortality.
CHIRPS and NASA SRTM: rainfall, and a derived altitude for each head town.

Start a new project folder beside the London one, start the assistant in it, and copy the data:



You do

cd ~ && mkdir -p water-quality && cd water-quality
claude



Ask your coding assistant

Copy ../quarto-workshop/examples/water/data into this folder as data/, then list the files in data/ with their sizes.


The folder holds water_municipal.csv (the analysis table), municipios.geojson (municipal boundaries for maps) and README.md, which documents every column, source, licence and caveat.
One row is one municipality’s urban or rural zone in one year. The urban zone is the head town (cabecera municipal); the rural zone is the smaller settlements and the dispersed countryside. The table covers every one of DANE’s 1,122 DIVIPOLA entries, both zones and every year from 2010 to 2023: 31,416 rows and 29 columns. Of those entries, 1,103 are municipalities; the rest are the island of San Andrés and areas that are not municipalities, whose rows are mostly empty. Because every municipality has all its rows, a gap is an empty cell, never a missing row.






TipIn practice



Read data/README.md before you analyse anything, and ask the assistant to read it first too. Its caveats are the analysis’s traps, written down: the IRCA source above; department capitals that have no urban and rural split for coverage; a fiscal index whose method changes in 2020; infant mortality whose method changes in 2017; Saber 11 only in some years; pesos that are not adjusted for inflation. Each one turns up in the chapters that follow.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.4 The question
The analysis asks two questions, in order:

Which kinds of municipal zone exist, judged by water safety, services and context?
How do health and education outcomes differ between those kinds?

“Kinds” will be clusters: groups of zone-years that are similar to each other on the chosen variables, found by an algorithm called k-means (Chapter 11). Because the unit is a zone in a year, a municipality’s two zones can belong to different kinds, and a zone can move between kinds over the years.
crumbs: Part III: One Analysis, Many Publications
8  The Question, the Data and the Rules

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.5 Features and outcomes
The most important design decision in Part III is which variables define the kinds and which only describe them.
The features, which the clustering sees, are 9 variables about water, people and place, and government: the utility-supplied IRCA, piped water and sewer coverage, the 2018 census’s multidimensional poverty index, the rural share of the population, the head town’s altitude, rainfall, a municipal performance index (MDM), and transfers for water per person (SGP, on a log scale). The outcomes, which the analysis only compares, are infant mortality, the Saber 11 score and school dropout.
Never cluster on an outcome. If infant mortality helped define the kinds, the kinds would differ in infant mortality by construction, and the comparison in the second question would be circular: it would find exactly what was put in. Keeping outcomes out of the clustering is what lets the comparison say anything at all.






NoteWhy this works



The split is also why the fiscal index idf is not a feature, although it describes municipal government: its method changes in 2020 (idf to 2020, idf_new from 2020, on different scales), so it cannot form one series across the years the analysis uses. A variable that changes meaning partway through would create kinds that are artefacts of the change.

title: 8  The Question, the Data and the Rules
text:
8.6 Compute once, publish many
Part II computed in each page. Part III computes once (Figure 8.1). One importable script, scripts/analysis.py, does all of the computation and writes its results to outputs/; every page only reads those results and draws them. A design choice, such as how many rows to drop for missing values, is made in one place, and every output follows at the next render.






Figure 8.1: Compute once, publish many. One script turns the data into results once; every publication reads the results, and none recomputes them.



The split solves two problems from Part II. A slow computation no longer slows every page and every format, because it runs once. And no page can disagree with another, because there is only one result to disagree with. Results are saved as Parquet, which keeps column types (a code such as 05001 stays text instead of becoming the number 5001), and as CSV where people will open them.
This book follows the same rule: every number in Part III is computed when the book is built, by importing the finished project’s analysis.py and running it in memory.

title: 9  Look Before You Model
text:
9.1 What exploring is for
Before any model, look at the data. Exploring tells you what a model will and will not be able to see: which columns are sparse, which zones are never measured, and whether a series changes level for reasons that have nothing to do with the thing it measures. None of that shows up as an error. A clustering algorithm will happily group rows that have been made comparable only by filling their gaps, and a chart of a series whose method changed will draw a trend that is not there.
This chapter does three things with the water data: it looks at how much is missing and where, it looks at how the IRCA moves over time, and it looks closely at one municipality, Tunja, to see what the caveats in the data’s README mean in practice. Then the assistant builds the project’s first page, explore.qmd.
Four questions are worth answering before modelling any table, and this chapter asks each of them of the water data:
The answers decide what the analysis can claim. If one group is mostly missing, conclusions about it rest on the minority that was measured, and that minority may not be typical.

How big is it? Rows and columns, and what one row is.
What is missing, and where? Missingness by column and by group (here, by zone).

9.2 Rural: less data, more risk








Figure 9.1: All rows, 2010–2023, by zone: no IRCA reported (hatched) and the Resolución 2115 risk band of the rest. Utility-supplied IRCA, INS open data (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3).





Figure 9.1 puts all 31,416 rows side by side. 53% of rural rows have no IRCA at all, against 14% of urban rows, because many rural systems are never sampled. Among the rural rows that do have a value, 51% fall in the high or unfit bands, against 12% of urban rows.
The two facts compound. Rural water is riskier where it is measured, and much of it is not measured. Missingness is not random: it is concentrated in small, remote, rural places. Any analysis that drops the rows without IRCA, as Part III’s must, describes sampled rural systems only, and should say so.








Figure 9.2: Median utility-supplied IRCA by year and zone, 2010–2023, over the rows that report one.





Figure 9.2 shows why the fourth question matters. The rural median drops sharply in 2016 and again in 2020. That could be an improvement in rural water, or a change in which systems were sampled; the data’s README warns that the 2020 drop may reflect sampling, and the open data cannot tell the two apart. An analysis that compares years should not read the drop as progress without evidence from outside the table.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.1 Four steps from table to features
A clustering algorithm does not read a table the way a person does. It sees numbers, measures distances between rows, and groups rows that are close. Everything about the result depends on which rows it sees, which numbers, on what scale, and what it is given where a number is missing. Preparation is the name for those decisions, and they shape the clusters as much as the algorithm does.
This chapter makes four decisions about the water data, explains each, and counts what each one costs in rows. Then the assistant writes them into scripts/analysis.py, the one script that every later page reads.
1. Select. Keep the years 2016 to 2023, because the municipal performance index (MDM), one of the features, starts in 2016. Keep municipalities only: San Andrés has none of DNP’s values and the non-municipalised areas are nearly empty. Keep only rows with an IRCA value, since water safety is the point of the analysis.
2. Transform. Transfers for water per person (SGP) are heavily skewed, with a few very large values, so the analysis uses their logarithm. Department capitals have no urban and rural split for coverage, so their urban rows use the municipality’s total coverage instead, and a flag column records that they did.
3. Impute, with flags. Drop rows missing more than two of the nine features. Fill the remaining gaps with the median of the same year and zone, and add a flag column, such as water_coverage_imputed, that marks every filled value.
4. Standardise within each year. Replace each feature by its z-score within its year:
\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}_{\text{year}}}{s_{\text{year}}}\]
where \(\bar{x}_{\text{year}}\) and \(s_{\text{year}}\) are the feature’s mean and standard deviation over that year’s kept rows. A z-score of +1 means one standard deviation above that year’s average.

NoteWhy this works



Why within each year rather than over all years? Two reasons. SGP is in nominal pesos, not adjusted for inflation, so its values drift upwards over time for reasons unrelated to any municipality. And other features shift as a whole from year to year. Standardising within each year removes both shifts, so a single clustering over all years gives labels that mean the same thing in 2016 and in 2023.








WarningCommon pitfall



Every fill is a guess, and an unflagged guess becomes indistinguishable from data. The flags make the guesses countable and checkable later: a cluster made mostly of imputed values would be a cluster of medians, not of places. The rule of the project, from its AGENTS.md: nothing is filled silently.

title: 10  From Table to Features
text:
10.3 Why scale?
k-means groups rows by straight-line, or Euclidean, distance: the square root of the sum of squared differences across the features. A feature’s share of that squared distance, between two rows picked at random, is proportional to its variance. In raw units, the features measured in thousands, such as millimetres of rain and metres of altitude, dwarf those measured from 0 to 100 (Figure 10.1).








Figure 10.1: Each feature’s share of the squared distance between rows, in raw units and after z-scores. Kept rows, 2016–2023.





Unscaled, rainfall and altitude together would make up 99.8% of the distance, so the clusters would be climate zones and the water variables would hardly count. After z-scores, every feature has variance 1 and contributes the same share, about 11%. The log of SGP matters too: with raw pesos, SGP alone would dominate.






TipIn practice



Equal weight is itself a choice, not a neutral default. Nine z-scored features count equally, so the three coverage-and-safety variables count for a third of the distance and context for the rest. If water safety should weigh more, that is a decision to make explicitly and report, not to leave to the units the data happened to come in.
